problem: Target-driven object navigation agents in AI2-THOR (e.g., SAVN, Scene Priors) have two weaknesses. First, their target representations are weak: GloVe or FastText word embeddings, or knowledge-graph priors from external databases, which are semantically ambiguous and carry no spatial information. Second, their pure-RL policies often fall into deadlock states (looping, repeating MoveAhead against an obstacle), and the reward gives no explicit signal for escaping them, either in training or in unseen test scenes.
motivation: Household objects co-occur strongly and in predictable spatial arrangements, e.g., TV next to remote or cushion on sofa. Learning these relations from detections lets an agent narrow its search when the target is small or not yet visible. Deadlocks are a major failure mode that RL rewards do not resolve, and expert supervision exists only in training. This motivates (a) imitation supervision applied only at failure states during training and (b) a learned module that imitates that supervision at test time.
key_idea: The method has three parts. A learned object relation graph over per-category Faster R-CNN detections serves as attention over local appearance features. Imitation learning from Dijkstra expert actions is applied only when the agent is in deadlock. A memory-augmented tentative policy network, trained to mimic that expert in deadlocks, issues escape actions at test time and updates the navigation policy.
insight: Detection-based target representation is the biggest single lever. Swapping word embeddings for detections lifts SAVN from 40.8 to 62.3 SR, and adding the learned relation graph on top of detections lifts the baseline from 56.4 SR / 0.319 SPL to 65.3 / 0.375. Removing ORG from the full model hurts SPL most (0.394→0.345), so relations mainly buy efficiency. Supervision must be targeted: IL at every step overfits badly (47.7 SR vs 63.6 with IL only at failed/deadlock states). Likewise, TPN applied at every state (66.2) or random escape actions (62.3) underperform deadlock-only TPN (69.3), showing that TPN learns a meaningful escape policy rather than just injecting randomness.
method: Location-aware feature (LAF): Faster R-CNN is retrained on AI2-THOR. For each of the N categories, the highest-confidence box coordinates and confidence are kept (zeros if the category is absent) and concatenated with a one-hot target vector. Location-aware appearance features are pooled from the detector backbone's 2nd ResBlock to keep spatial detail.

Object Relation Graph (ORG): a GCN Z = ReLU(A·X·W) over the per-category LAF nodes. Both the node embedding W and the adjacency A are learned from the training environments, with no external knowledge base, so the graph encodes category closeness and spatial correlation.

Graph attention layer: the parameter-free F̂ = ReLU(Z·F) uses ORG as an attention map over the N×512 appearance features. The result is concatenated with the LAF and fused with an ImageNet-pretrained ResNet18 global feature of the current view.

Navigation policy: A3C with an LSTM. Input is the visual representation plus the previous action and state embedding, both spatially tiled. Rewards are -0.001 per step and +5 on success; training uses 12 asynchronous agents for 6M episodes with Adam at lr 1e-4.

Trial-driven IL: cross-entropy toward Dijkstra shortest-path expert actions, applied only in deadlock states. Total loss is L = L_nav + L_il, which keeps episodes going without overfitting the seen rooms.

Memory-augmented TPN: an external vision memory flags a deadlock when the current visual feature matches a previously recorded one. An internal memory stores (state key f_t; value = action a_t, next state f_t+1). Soft attention (softmax of inner products) over the internal memory yields an embedded memory feature, which is concatenated with the current state to predict an escape action. TPN is trained for 2M episodes with IL labels in deadlocks while the navigator is frozen. At test time the frozen TPN's action supervises the base policy via L_tpn cross-entropy, i.e., the policy is updated at test time.

setting.backbone: Faster R-CNN detector (retrained on AI2-THOR) + ResNet18 (ImageNet-pretrained) global features + learned GCN (ORG) + A3C LSTM policy + TPN, policy trained from scratch with RL + IL
setting.training_data: AI2-THOR (iTHOR) training rooms: 4 scene types (kitchen, living room, bedroom, bathroom), 22 target categories following SAVN; 25 of 30 rooms per scene type used for train+val. Navigation policy trained for 6M episodes; TPN for a further 2M episodes. Detector trained on half of the training data with augmentation. Dijkstra shortest-path expert actions used as IL labels.
setting.action_space: discrete grid actions: MoveAhead, RotateLeft, RotateRight, LookUp, LookDown, Done (max 99 steps per case study)
setting.privileged: none at test time (Dijkstra expert used only in training). Note: TPN performs test-time gradient updates of the navigation policy.

numbers.backbone: Faster R-CNN + ResNet18 + ORG GCN + A3C LSTM + TPN
numbers.extra: SAVN protocol, unseen test rooms (20 rooms across 4 scene types); success = Done within 1.5 m with target visible; TPN updates the policy at test time; SR/SPL L≥5 = episodes with optimal path ≥5 steps

numbers.backbone: Faster R-CNN + ResNet18 + ORG GCN + A3C LSTM
numbers.evidence: Table 2 'Impacts of different components on navigation performances': w/o TPN 66.6% 0.387 / 57.4% 0.374

numbers.backbone: Faster R-CNN + ResNet18 + ORG GCN + A3C LSTM

numbers_note: The paper prints SPL on a 0-1 scale (e.g., 0.394); values are converted to 0-100 here. The benchmark is the SAVN iTHOR protocol, which is not in the canonical list. The number of test episodes is not stated. The headline '22.8% increase' in SR is relative (56.4→69.3), not absolute.
results: On unseen AI2-THOR rooms the full model reaches 69.3% SR / 0.394 SPL (60.7% / 0.386 on paths ≥5 steps). This beats the detection-based baseline (56.4 / 0.319) and the strongest re-implemented baselines D-SAVN (62.3 / 0.264) and D-SP (59.6 / 0.303). The original SAVN (40.8 / 0.161) and Scene Priors (35.1 / 0.155) are far behind. Each component helps on its own: +ORG 65.3, +IL 63.6, +TPN 58.7 SR over the 56.4 baseline.
limitations: Evaluated only in small single-room iTHOR scenes on a discrete grid, with a closed set of 22 categories and a detector retrained on the same simulator. No multi-room houses, continuous control, or real robot.

Deadlock detection relies on exact or near-identical visual feature repeats, which suits a discrete grid. TPN also performs gradient updates of the policy at test time, which complicates comparison with purely feed-forward methods.
The strongest baselines (D-SP, D-SAVN) are the authors' own re-implementations with detection inputs. There is little analysis of detector errors or of the sensitivity of the learned adjacency.
